content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem's symptom statement and starting the causal chain, noting how account page error rates spiked from baseline to a peak value, citing the relevant graphs and tickets.

For the "why" steps, I'm tracing the root cause to a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py triggered between 14:22-14:28, which I'm linking back to the monthly-spend-feature flag being enabled and gradually routing more traffic (half, then all) through the new spend summary path. I'm also working through ruling out alternative causes — checking that no deploys occurred, confirming only one flag change happened that day, and evaluating whether the pre-existing ClientDisconnected errors were just baseline noise rather than a contributing factor.

Confirming the revert with T19, T21, T22, M1 for step 3's citations. For step 4, I'm tracing why the new path raised an error: F1 shows average_spend_per_item_this_month dividing by an empty list without a check, which applies to shoppers with no purchases this month — G5309's ZeroDivisionError at line 47 supports the division-by-zero but not specifically the empty-list cause, so this counts as an unrun reading that still reaches a cause. For step 5, I'm looking at why this was missed, tied to the lifetime-average reasoning where the divisor is only empty for shoppers who never purchased.

Root cause: the new monthly spend summary divides by the count of this month's purchases without an empty-list guard, so shoppers with past purchases but none this month hit a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 and their account page fails — the missing guard stems from reusing lifetime-average logic where that edge case couldn't occur.

The flag being off now doesn't fix the underlying bug; re-enabling monthly spend would likely break account pages again for the same no-purchase-this-month shoppers, since the division fault is still in the code.

Contributing factors: CF-1 — the rollout wasn't a clean all-at-once flip; G971b shows 97 accounts on / 103 off at minute 14:22 before converging to full rollout.

F1's test file labels this the ordinary case, and the new tests are written to fail against the current code—meaning nothing previously covered it, which AI-2's fix now addresses; had that gap not existed, the fault would've been caught before the flag went live.

CF-3 overlaps with CF-2 so I'll skip it. For CF-4, nobody got paged, but that's really a detection and alert-routing issue rather than a condition that would have changed the outcome—Argus mitigated quickly regardless, so I'm inclined to skip this one too.

I'm also considering whether the admin who toggled the flag lacked any review step, but that overlaps with CF-1, so I'll consolidate around CF-1 (staged rollout with automatic halt) and CF-2 (test coverage) as the main contributing factors, skipping the alert-timing nuance since detection speed isn't clearly the bottleneck here.

For action items, I'm drafting: a staged rollout proposal starting with a small share of traffic (CF-1, prevent), an automatic halt/revert trigger when account page errors exceed baseline (CF-1, mitigate), and a process requirement that flag-gated paths be tested with the flag on—including edge cases like a shopper with no purchases in the current month—before production activation (CF-2). I'm also weighing whether to suggest auditing other monthly calculations in spend_summary.py for similar empty-month division issues, though that may be outside the scope of what the files actually show.

For the lessons section, I'm noting that Argus reverted the flag after the alert fired and confirmed the revert restored service, that the investigator linked the flag change to the incident onset via evaluation logs, and that Code-Fix proposed a draft fix with tests in PR #361 — I want to name what was proposed without detailing its contents. For what went wrong, I'm considering whether the lack of a paged on-call engineer counts, since Argus handled the response autonomously, and how to phrase that observation.

I'm deciding that the flag going live without a staged rollout is a contributing factor rather than luck, and leaving "got lucky" empty since the limited blast radius was due to the nature of the bug rather than chance. For assumptions, I'm noting that the ZeroDivisionError count of 13 in the logs is likely a sample rather than the complete picture, so I shouldn't treat it as fully representative of all failed requests, and I'm also flagging the assumption that failing shoppers specifically had past purchases but none this month.

I want to avoid writing raw numbers in the prose, so for the line reference in spend_summary.py I'll use the figure label notation instead of the literal line number.

For step 1, I'm noting the citations showing user-facing failure: the account page error rate, the failed account page request, and the metrics source, with before/during/peak error rate figures referenced by label. For step 3's timeline, I'm tracking when the flag switched on, the mixed evaluation state, when it went fully on, when it was fully off, and the revert and confirmation times, all referenced by their figure labels rather than literal numbers.

I also rule out deploy as a cause, citing the replica revision data, and ClientDisconnected, citing the normal rendering logs and metrics baseline. I note that only one flag change by someone other than Argus occurred in the hour before, citing that history log as evidence there wasn't another contributing flag change.

Now I need to write the final answer avoiding exact numbers — words like "half" count as forbidden figures, so I'll reference the on/off figures by their labels instead.

action_items.item: Roll out io-shop feature flag changes in production in stages, starting with a small share of traffic.
Halt and revert an io-shop flag rollout automatically when the account-page error rate rises above its baseline during the rollout.
Require tests that exercise a flag-gated code path with the flag on before that flag can be switched on in production.
Review the other per-month figures in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py for divisions by a count that can be empty in a month.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The share of requests that failed rose from {errors_before} before the onset to {errors_while_broken} while it was broken, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The service's own account-page error warnings were highest at {Gbac1.7}.
From {G5309.3}, account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py.

ruled_out.what: A deploy: the production change events read for the day before the onset returned only the flag change and no deploys. At {T10.1}, every replica ran a single revision.
Another flag change: at {T16.1}, the flag provider's history for the hour before showed only one flag change by anyone but Argus, which was this one.
Shoppers closing the connection: these ClientDisconnected failures were logged from {G46bc.3}, starting well before the onset, while the metrics read showed the service at its baseline error rate.

causal_chain.step: The new spend summary code path was running because an admin switched on the feature flag monthly-spend-feature at {P1.1}. Up to {G7e5d.4} every flag evaluation was off. In the minute {G971b.6}, evaluations split {G971b.2} on and {G971b.1} off, and from {Gce95.4} every evaluation was on. Switching the flag off at {T19.1} brought the service back to normal by {T21.2}, and the action was judged confirmed at {T22.1}.

According to Code-Fix's reading of the source, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` divides `account.total_this_month_cents` by `len(bought_this_month)` without checking that the list is non-empty. For a shopper who has bought before but not in the current month, that list is empty, so the function raises ZeroDivisionError.

The check is missing because the reasoning behind the lifetime average was carried over to the month. The lifetime average's docstring says its divisor is empty only for an account that never bought anything, which no real shopper is. That does not hold for a single month, where an empty divisor is common.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new monthly spending summary on shoppers' account pages exposed a calculation that likely divides by the number of purchases a shopper made this month without allowing for shoppers who bought nothing this month, so their account pages failed.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag change reached every evaluation within moments: first a split between on and off, then on for all. No staged rollout and no automatic halt on a rising error rate were seen for the flag change.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A staged rollout that halts on a rising account-page error rate would have exposed only a small share of shoppers and stopped or reverted the flag before most account pages failed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen that runs the monthly spend path for a shopper who has earlier purchases but none this month, even though the test file Code-Fix read calls this kind of shopper the ordinary case. Code-Fix's new tests for that case are written to raise ZeroDivisionError against the current code.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test of this case would have failed before the flag was switched on, so the fault would have been found without any shopper seeing it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well: The Investigator tied the onset to the flag change by matching the flag-evaluation log lines, which switched from off to on, against the ZeroDivisionError lines that began in the same minute.
Argus switched monthly-spend-feature off {T19.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Argus confirmed {T22.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised that switching off the flag had brought the service back.
Code-Fix proposed a fix, with tests, as draft pull request PR #361.
went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was told while the incident ran.

input.root_cause: The monthly spend summary path that monthly-spend-feature turns on calls `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. That function divides the month's total by the number of purchases made this month and never checks whether there were any. So for any shopper who has bought before but not this month, it raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} and their account page fails. The check is missing because the reasoning behind the lifetime average was carried over to a single month: the lifetime divisor is empty only for an account that never bought anything, but a month's divisor is often empty.
input.still_at_risk: The flag is off, but the faulty monthly spend calculation is still in the code, so switching monthly-spend-feature back on would likely make account pages fail again for shoppers with no purchases this month.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
